newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbian authorities force independent TV off air.
newsitem.headline: Serbian authorities force independent TV off air.

text.p: The most trusted and popular television station in Serbia has been blacked out across most of the country amid a fierce battle for control of the media ahead of elections later this year.

The state telecommunications authority cut independent BK TV's transmission lines going south from Belgrade on Thursday evening, stopping its broadcasts to cities south of the capital, Velimir Zugic, BK's technical manager, said on Friday.
"We are now only covering Belgrade and northern parts of Serbia -- cities like Novi Sad," he said.
"We have now been halved in coverage. That means in future, unless we find another solution we are going to be really a local station, not a national station."
According to a recent poll, BK TV was rated the most watched and most trusted station in the country by far.
"Probably that is the reason which prompted the government to reduce our coverage in Serbia," Zugic said.
But hours later a Belgrade court ordered both the telecommunications authority and state-run Serbian television network RTS to air BK on its transmitters.
"If they do not obey the court then all their claims that this is a country ruled by law will be dashed," Zugic said.
Early this month RTS warned BK TV it could no longer count on its transmitters to broadcast outside Belgrade, citing financial reasons.
BK TV called the move the "most flagrant attack on media freedom in Serbia and the right of citizens to be informed".
It came after a political upheaval in Serbia caused by election fraud last November by the ruling Socialist Party (SPS) of Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic.

Huge demonstrations by Serbia's Zajedno (Together) coalition of opposition groups, drawing up to 500,000 at their peak, forced Milosevic to restore local election victories in 14 cities, including Belgrade.
The widespread protests were the biggest-ever challenge to Milosevic's 10-year rule.

The opposition demands free access to the media which the SPS, fighting to reinstate its battered popularity ahead of presidential and parliamentary elections later this year, is loath to concede despite heavy pressure from the West.
The United States has retained an outer wall of sanctions against Belgrade, barring Milosevic from desperately needed foreign capital to resuscitate his moribund economy.

Belgrade's commitment to democracy, human rights and freedom of the press is one of the conditions for the sanctions to be lifted, and the latest stifling of the media will diminsh chances of that happening in time for Milosevic to score election points.
BK TV's owner Bogoljub Karic had been one of Milosevic's closest allies but fell out with him after the November election fiasco.

Karic, whom analysts see as a potential presidential contender, criticised Milosevic for mishandling the affair. He said he backed any force seeking to reintegrate Serbia into the world as a modern, democratic and free market society.
Milosevic's popularity plummeted from 32 percent to 13 percent in February opinion polls.
Western diplomats believe Milosevic will not even run for the presidency of Serbia but opt instead for the post of Yugoslav federal president.
